title: Why Mumbai Floods Every Single Monsoon
creator: Arjun Mehta Explains
description:
India's richest city goes underwater almost every July. Here's why, and why it's so hard to fix.

Data: BMC flood preparedness reports, IMD rainfall archive, Fact-Finding Committee report on the 2005 floods.

sentences.t: On the twenty-sixth of July, 2005, Mumbai got nearly a meter of rain in a single day.
Nine hundred and forty four millimeters, which is more than London gets in an entire year.
More than a thousand people died across the state, and the city basically stopped for three days.
And here's the thing, it wasn't a freak event that never came back.
Smaller versions of that day happen almost every single monsoon.
Trains stop, Andheri subway fills up like a swimming pool, and people wade home through water up to their waist.
So why does this keep happening in one of the richest cities in Asia?
Let's start with geography, because Mumbai was never really supposed to be one city.
It started as seven separate islands, with marshes and creeks and mangroves in between.
Over about two hundred years, the British and then the Indian government filled in all of that land to join them together.
Which means large parts of the city sit on reclaimed ground that's barely above sea level.
Now add the tides.
Mumbai's storm drains empty straight into the sea.
But when a heavy downpour hits during high tide, the sea level is higher than the drain outlets.
So the gates have to close, and the rainwater has nowhere to go.
If you get a few hours of heavy rain at high tide, that's it, the low-lying areas flood, no matter how clean the drains are.
I actually saw this happen last July from my own building in Sion.
I was standing on the balcony filming on my old Redmi phone, which honestly barely survived the humidity that year.
And you could literally watch the water rise on the road in the time it took my tea to go cold.
Then the second problem, and this one is man-made.
The drainage system in the old city was designed more than a hundred years ago for about twenty-five millimeters of rain an hour.
On a bad monsoon day, Mumbai gets three or four times that.
And a lot of the drains are clogged with plastic and construction debris before the season even starts.
Third problem, the Mithi River.
Most people in Mumbai don't even know it's a river, because for decades it was treated like an open sewer.
It was narrowed, built over, and the airport runway was extended right across part of its path.
So when it fills up in a storm, it doesn't drain, it just spills into the neighborhoods around it.
And fourth, the mangroves.
Mangroves are basically a natural sponge along the coast, they soak up storm surge and slow the water down.
Mumbai has lost a huge share of its mangroves to construction, and every hectare that goes makes the next flood a little worse.
So can it be fixed?
Partly, yes.
After 2005, the city started a big project to widen the main storm drains and build pumping stations that push water out even at high tide.
Where those pumping stations are finished, flooding has genuinely gone down.
But the project is years behind schedule, and several stations are still stuck in court cases and land disputes.
And none of it works if the drains are full of plastic every June.
Honestly, the most effective things are also the least exciting, cleaning the drains on time, protecting what's left of the mangroves, and not building on flood plains.
In the next video, we'll look at Chennai, which has almost the opposite problem, too little water most of the year and then far too much all at once.
If you've been stuck in a Mumbai flood, tell me your story in the comments.
See you next time.
